newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli PM wins go-ahead for unblemished top lawyer.
newsitem.headline: Israeli PM wins go-ahead for unblemished top lawyer.

text.p: Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu, whose previous choice of attorney-general got the government entangled in a criminal inquiry, won cabinet approval on Wednesday for an unblemished replacement.

Elyakim Rubinstein, a 49-year-old Jerusalem court judge, won praise for his service as cabinet secretary in governments left and right and made history as a peacemaker with Egypt, Jordan and the Palestinians.

"The government has unanimously decided...to appoint Judge Elyakim Rubinstein to the position of attorney-general," Netanyahu's cabinet said in a statement. The appointment takes effect on February 12.
Israel's police fraud squad opened an investigation this week into alleged corruption in the appointment earlier this month of lawyer Roni Bar-On as attorney-general.

Bar-On quit 12 hours after taking office as debate swirled over charges he got the job more for his loyalty to Netanyahu's Likud party than his legal acumen. An Israeli television report gave rise to charges the appointment was criminal as well as poor judgment.

Tel Aviv-born Rubinstein was hailed by politicians left and right as a quick wit and a straight arrow. The cabinet approved his appointment despite his refusal to take a polygraph test required by Israel's Shin Bet secret security service.
Israel Radio's legal correspondent Moshe Negbi said Rubinstein had refused to take the test for a previous appointment on grounds it violated his privacy.
Rubinstein declined comment ahead of the cabinet vote.
But during a lecture in northern Israel on Wednesday on Israel's peace treaty with Jordan, he complained about having just had a tooth pulled -- "and an attorney-general needs teeth in particular".

State-run Channel One Television reported last week that Bar-On's appointment had been part of a deal with ultra-Orthodox Shas party leader Aryeh Deri, a political kingmaker on trial for corruption since 1993.

It said Deri demanded Bar-On get the job in return for Shas party support for Netanyahu's accord with the PLO on the West Bank town of Hebron, completed this month. It said Bar-On promised Deri a plea-bargain that would let Deri continue his political career.
Netanyahu, elected only eight months ago, has denied the charges along with Bar-On and Deri.

In another legal development that could plague the government, police said they had begun an investigation into complaints the prime minister's director-general Avigdor Liberman knowingly gave the cabinet incorrect information about the Israel Broadcasting Authority budget ahead of a vote.

Liberman, speaking to Israel Television Channel Two on Wednesday, attacked the police as "a political battering ram, a means to settle scores." He dismissed the allegations regarding Deri and Bar-On as an "unsuccessful joke."

Internal Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani said he would ask Liberman to retract his remarks. Kahalani said his "gut feeling" was that the Bar-On charges were "more shouting than substance." But, in an interview on Channel One, he added:
"If the things said on Channel One are true, this government has no place. If they are true, we have to go to new elections."
